'''Nathan Keyfitz''' <small>[[Royal Society of Canada|FRSC]]</small> <small>[[Royal Statistical Society|FRSS]]</small> (June 29, 1913 – April 6, 2010) was a [[Canadians|Canadian]] [[demography|demographer]], a pioneer of mathematical demography.<ref name="gazette">{{citation|title=Professor Nathan Keyfitz dies at 96|journal=Harvard Gazette|date=April 9, 2010|url=http://news.harvard.edu/gazette/story/2010/04/nathan-keyfitz-dies-at-96/}}.</ref><ref name="ep">{{citation|contribution=Keyfitz, Nathan|title=Encyclopedia of Population|date=January 1, 2003|url=http://www.highbeam.com/doc/1G2-3403900199.html|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150329111825/http://www.highbeam.com/doc/1G2-3403900199.html|url-status=usurped|archive-date=March 29, 2015|url-access=subscription |first=Jacques|via=[[HighBeam Research]]|last=Ledent}}.</ref><ref name="iiasa">{{citation|title=In Memoriam Nathan Keyfitz|first=Peter E.|last=de Janosi|url=http://society.iiasa.ac.at/index.php/archive/233-in-memoriam-nathan-keyfitz|date=June 8, 2010|publisher=The IIASA Society|accessdate=2013-01-27|url-status=dead|archiveurl=https://web.archive.org/web/20120606033347/http://society.iiasa.ac.at/index.php/archive/233-in-memoriam-nathan-keyfitz|archivedate=June 6, 2012}}.</ref><ref name="tribute">{{citation|title=Tribute to Nathan Keyfitz|journal=Canadian Studies in Population|volume=37|issue=3–4|first=Barry|last=Edmonston|year=2010 |url=http://ejournals.library.ualberta.ca/index.php/csp/article/view/16038|pages=vii–ix|doi=10.25336/P6KC9G |doi-access=free}}.</ref><ref name="ledent">{{citation|title=In Memoriam : Nathan Keyfitz 1913-2010|first=Jacques|last=Ledent|journal=Cahiers Québécois de Démographie|language=French|volume=39|issue=2|year=2010|pages=399–400|doi=10.7202/1003593ar|doi-access=free}}.</ref>

==Professional career==
Keyfitz studied at [[McGill University]], graduating with a B.S. in [[mathematics]] in 1934.<ref name="gazette"/><ref name="ep"/><ref name="tribute"/> He worked for the [[Statistics Canada|Dominion Bureau of Statistics]] in Canada from 1936 to 1959, meanwhile earning a Ph.D. in [[sociology]] from the [[University of Chicago]] in 1952.<ref name="ep"/><ref name="tribute"/> In 1959, he took a professorship at the [[University of Toronto]]; he moved from there to the University of Chicago and the [[University of California, Berkeley]] before joining the faculty of [[Harvard University]] as Andelot Professor of Sociology in 1972. From 1978 to 1980 he served as Director of the [http://www.hsph.harvard.edu/cpds Harvard Center for Population and Development Studies]. He retired from Harvard in 1981, only to take another faculty position at [[Ohio State University]] and then to direct the Population Program at the [[International Institute for Applied Systems Analysis]] in Austria from 1983 to 1993.<ref name="gazette"/><ref name="ep"/><ref name="tribute"/> He also consulted frequently in [[Indonesia]] over a period of many years.<ref name="ep"/>

He was president of the [[Population Association of America]] from 1970 to 1971.<ref name="ep"/>

==Awards and honors==
Keyfitz was a fellow of the [[Royal Society of Canada]], the [[Royal Statistical Society]], the [[American Statistical Association]], and the [[American Academy of Arts and Sciences]], and a member of the [[National Academy of Sciences|U.S. National Academy of Sciences]].<ref name="gazette"/><ref name="ep"/><ref name="tribute"/><ref name="footnotes"/> He was given seven honorary doctorates,<ref name="tribute"/> won the Mindel C. Sheps Award of the Population Association of America in 1976,<ref name="ep"/><ref>[http://www.populationassociation.org/sidebar/annual-meeting/awards/mindel-sheps-award-past-recipients/ Award Criteria and  Recipients: Mindel C. Sheps Award], Population Association of America, retrieved 2013-01-27.</ref> and won the Common Wealth Award of Distinguished Service in 1991.<ref name="footnotes">{{citation|title=Keyfitz Named 1991 Common Wealth Award Winner|journal=Footnotes|publisher=American Sociological Association|volume=19|issue=3|date=March 1991|url=http://www.asanet.org/footnotes/1991/asa.03.1991.pdf|pages=1,&nbsp;9|url-status=dead|archiveurl=https://web.archive.org/web/20120802113100/http://www.asanet.org/footnotes/1991/ASA.03.1991.pdf|archivedate=2012-08-02}}.</ref>

In June 2013, a symposium on mathematical demography was held in honor of the centennial of his birth.<ref>[http://www.mbi.osu.edu/2012/keydescription.html The Keyfitz Centennial Symposium on Mathematical Demography (June 24-28, 2013)], retrieved 2013-01-027.</ref>

==Books==
*''Introduction to the Mathematics of Population'' (Addison-Wesley, 1968). {{ISBN|978-0-201-53167-1}}.
*''World Population: An Analysis of Vital Data'' (with Wilhelm Flieger, Univ. of Chicago Press, 1968). {{ISBN|978-0-226-43234-2}}.
*''Population: Facts and Methods of Demography'' (with Wilhelm Flieger, W.H. Freeman and Company, 1971)
*''Applied Mathematical Demography'' (Springer-Verlag, 1977)
*''Population Change and Social Policy'' (Abt Books, 1982)
*''World Population Growth and Aging: Demographic Trends in the Late Twentieth Century'' (with Wilhelm Flieger, Univ. of Chicago Press, 1990)

==Personal==
Keyfitz's daughter, [[Barbara Keyfitz]], is a notable mathematician.
